title: AI Use-Case Selection
summary: Which problems AI is actually good at — and the far larger set it is not.
what: Use-case selection is deciding where AI belongs in a product. The decision turns on the shape of the problem: how tolerant it is of error, whether output can be verified, and whether the task is genuinely one a language model does well.
why: Most failed AI features did not fail on execution. They failed because the problem was a poor fit and no amount of engineering was going to change that.
analogy: Choosing where to use a power tool. Extremely effective on the right material; on the wrong material it is fast, confident and destructive.
technical:
**Good fit** has a recognisable shape:
- The task is **language-shaped** — summarising, extracting, classifying, drafting, translating between formats.
- **Errors are recoverable** and preferably visible.
- **Output can be verified** by the person receiving it, or by the system.
- There is **variety** the rules-based alternative cannot cover.
- The **status quo is bad** — a slow manual process, or nothing at all.

**Poor fit** is equally recognisable:
- **Exact answers required** — arithmetic, totals, compliance determinations. A model that is right 97% of the time on a calculation is not useful; a calculator is right 100% of the time.
- **A deterministic rule already works.** If the logic fits in an if-statement, use the if-statement — it is cheaper, faster, testable and explainable.
- **Errors are silent and consequential.** The combination is what makes a use case dangerous, not either alone.
- **Nobody can tell whether the output is right.** Unverifiable output in a high-stakes context is the single worst shape.

**The reframe that saves most projects:** ask not "can AI do this task?" but "which part of this workflow is language-shaped, and which part should stay deterministic?" Almost every good AI feature is a hybrid — the model handles the messy language part and hands off to code for anything that must be exact.

questions.q: What shape of problem is a good fit for AI?
questions.a: Language-shaped tasks — summarising, extracting, classifying, drafting — where errors are recoverable and visible, output can be verified by the recipient, and the variety defeats a rules-based alternative.

interview.s90: The reframe I use most is to stop asking whether AI can do the task and start asking which part of the workflow is language-shaped and which part must stay deterministic. A team asked me for AI-calculated refund amounts. Calculation is arithmetic on policy rules — a model that is right 97% of the time is worse than a rule engine that is right every time, and the errors are silent and financial. But the part that was genuinely hard was extracting the facts from a messy support thread: order date, item condition, stated reason. So the model extracts, and deterministic code applies the policy. That version shipped and works. The one they asked for would have failed, and it would have failed on the problem shape rather than on execution — which is true of most AI features that do not work.

title: AI Feasibility
summary: Finding out whether the model can actually do it, before committing a quarter to it.
what: Feasibility assessment establishes whether a model can perform a task at the quality your product requires, using your real data, measured against a real bar.
why: It is the risk that distinguishes AI product work from conventional product work. In normal software, a specification you can write is one you can build. Here, the answer might simply be no, and finding that out in week one costs three days rather than a quarter.
analogy: Drilling a test core before committing to a mine. Cheap, unglamorous, and the only thing standing between a plan and an expensive hole.
technical:
The method — a **spike**, timeboxed to two to five days:

1. **Collect twenty to fifty real examples**, not invented ones. Include the hard cases; real traffic is not uniformly easy.
2. **Define the bar first.** What error rate would make this shippable? Agreeing that after seeing results is how projects talk themselves into bad numbers.
3. **Build the crudest possible pipeline.** No optimisation, no framework, no infrastructure. You are measuring the ceiling, not the product.
4. **Score by hand** against ground truth, and split by difficulty.
5. **Decide**: proceed, improve a specific thing and re-measure, or stop.

**The result is a number and a distribution, not an impression.** "It seemed pretty good" is the failure mode. Twenty examples scored by hand takes an afternoon and produces something arguable.

**Read the failures, not just the score.** The most valuable output of a spike is usually the *kind* of error. Twenty percent failure caused by bad PDF parsing is a fixable engineering problem; twenty percent failure caused by the model misunderstanding the domain is not, at least not cheaply.

**A negative result is a successful spike.** Three days spent proving something is not currently feasible is one of the highest-return activities available to an AI product team, and it is systematically undervalued because it produces no demo.

questions.q: Why does feasibility come first for AI features?
questions.a: In conventional software a specification you can write is one you can build. With AI the answer may be no, and a three-day spike finds that out instead of a quarter of engineering.

questions.q: Why read the failures rather than the score?
questions.a: The same score means opposite things. Twenty percent failure from bad PDF parsing is a fixable engineering problem; twenty percent from the model misunderstanding the domain is not.

questions.q: Why must the quality bar be agreed before the spike runs?
questions.a: Defining it afterwards lets the team rationalise whatever number came back. Agreeing it in writing beforehand is what makes the result a decision rather than a negotiation.

interview.s30: Feasibility assessment is finding out whether the model can actually do the task at the quality the product needs, before committing engineering time. It is the risk that makes AI product work different from ordinary product work.
interview.s90: In normal software, if you can write the specification you can usually build it. With AI the answer might simply be no, and the cheapest way to find that out is a two- to five-day spike on twenty to forty real examples with the quality bar agreed in writing beforehand. On a policy-answer feature our spike came back at 22.5% confidently wrong, which reads as "not feasible". But reading the failures rather than the score changed the decision entirely: six of nine failures were ingestion problems — tables the PDF parser had dropped and regional documents we simply did not have — not the model misunderstanding the domain. So the first two sprints became fixing ingestion rather than building the feature, and the re-spike came back at 3.1%.
interview.technical: The spike is deliberately crude: naive chunking, no reranking, no framework. You are measuring the ceiling, not the product, and optimisation at this stage measures your effort rather than what is achievable. Score by hand against ground truth and split by difficulty, because averaged scores hide the shape. Then categorise the failures — retrieval failure, missing source, chunk boundary, model error — because the same score means opposite things depending on the mix.
interview.pm: It is the cheapest decision-quality improvement available: three days of work that can prevent a quarter spent building something that cannot work, and a negative result is a successful spike even though it produces no demo.
interview.example: A support-assistant spike, forty real questions, three days. Result 22.5% confidently wrong; failure analysis showed two-thirds of the errors were table-heavy documents the parser silently dropped. Fixing ingestion first took twelve days and brought it to 3.1%.

title: AI Model Selection
summary: Choosing on measured performance for your task, not on benchmarks or reputation.
what: Model selection is choosing which model serves a given feature, on the basis of measured quality against your own evaluation set, alongside cost, latency, data handling and operational constraints.
why: It is a decision teams make from leaderboards and vibes, and then live with for a year. Public benchmarks describe average performance on tasks that are not yours, and the ranking on your task is routinely different.
analogy: Hiring on a general aptitude test rather than a work sample. The test correlates with something; the work sample tells you whether they can do the job.
technical:
The criteria, in order of decisiveness:
1. **Measured quality on your golden set**, broken down by task category. This dominates everything else.
2. **Cost per interaction at your volume**, including retries and the input tokens your context assembly actually sends.
3. **Latency at your percentiles**, particularly time to first token if you stream.
4. **Data handling** — where processing happens, retention policy, contractual terms. Frequently the constraint that eliminates options before quality is even considered.
5. **Operational fit** — rate limits, availability, versioning behaviour, deprecation notice.

**Benchmarks are a shortlist tool, not a decision tool.** Use them to pick three candidates; use your own evaluation to choose between them.

**Test the smallest plausible model first.** Teams start at the top of the range and never check downward. On extraction and classification a small model frequently matches a large one at a fraction of the cost and latency — and the only way to know is to measure by task category, because the gap is narrow on some tasks and wide on others.

**Design for substitution.** Keep model choice behind an interface, keep prompts versioned, and keep the evaluation set current. A team that can swap models in an afternoon can take advantage of every release; a team that cannot is locked to whatever it launched with.

# ── STEP 0: THE CONSTRAINT THAT ELIMINATES CANDIDATES ──────
# Enterprise contract requires: no training on our data,
# configurable retention, and a documented processing region.
# This removed two of five candidates before any quality
# measurement — and it is the step teams do last.

CANDIDATES = ["large-hosted", "mid-hosted", "small-hosted", "local-8b"]

def select(golden_set, candidates, volume_per_month):
    rows = []
    for name in candidates:
        by_cat, lat, cost = {}, [], []
        for case in golden_set:
            out = run(case, name)
            by_cat.setdefault(case["category"], []).append(score(case, out))
            lat.append(out["latency_ms"]); cost.append(out["cost"])
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            **{c: round(sum(s)/len(s), 2) for c, s in by_cat.items()},
            "p95_ms": sorted(lat)[int(len(lat)*.95)],
            "monthly": round(sum(cost)/len(cost) * volume_per_month),
        })
    return rows

for r in select(GOLDEN, CANDIDATES, 240_000):
    print(r)

title: AI Build vs Buy
summary: What to buy, what to build, and the one layer you should never outsource.
what: The build-versus-buy decision for AI systems: which layers to take as a service, which to run yourself, and which to treat as core intellectual property.
why: The layers are unusually separable here, so the answer is rarely all-or-nothing. Teams that decide at the level of "build an AI product or buy one" get it wrong; teams that decide per layer usually get it right.
analogy: A restaurant. You buy the ovens and the electricity, you might buy the bread, and you never outsource the recipe.
technical:
Layer by layer:

**Buy the model.** Training a foundation model is not a realistic option, and for the overwhelming majority of products, fine-tuning is not either. Model capability is available to your competitors on the same terms, which is precisely why it is not where advantage lives.

**Buy commodity infrastructure** — vector storage, tracing backends, serving. These are solved problems with good options.

**Build your data pipeline.** Your corpus, its parsing, its metadata and its freshness are specific to you and largely determine quality. This is where the differentiated work is, and it is unglamorous enough that it gets skipped.

**Build your evaluation.** This is the one layer never to outsource. Your golden set encodes what quality means for your product; it is the asset that lets you change models, upgrade safely and improve faster than a competitor. Tooling can be bought; the cases and the judgement cannot.

**Buy the application only when the workflow is generic** — a standard chatbot, a standard summariser. The moment your workflow is specific, the integration cost of a generic product exceeds building the thin layer yourself.

**The failure mode with buying an end-to-end AI product** is that you cannot evaluate it. If you cannot run your own golden set against a vendor's system, you cannot tell whether it degraded after their last update, and you have outsourced the one thing you needed to keep.

title: AI Product Roadmap
summary: Sequencing work when the central uncertainty is whether it will work at all.
what: An AI product roadmap sequences capability work, quality infrastructure and rollout, in an order that resolves uncertainty before committing to it.
why: A conventional roadmap assumes the main risk is time. Here the main risk is whether the thing works, so the sequencing that makes sense is different — and the quality infrastructure that looks like overhead is what determines whether the roadmap survives.
analogy: Building the measuring instruments before the experiment. It feels like a detour until you realise every subsequent decision depends on being able to measure.
technical:
The sequencing that works:

**Phase 0 — feasibility.** A spike, before anything is committed. The roadmap item is the spike, not the feature.

**Phase 1 — evaluation infrastructure.** The golden set, the scoring, the regression harness. This looks like overhead and it is what everything else depends on. A team without it cannot tell whether a change helped, cannot upgrade a model, and cannot detect degradation.

**Phase 2 — the narrowest useful slice.** One category, one workflow, behind a flag, with abstention and error reporting from the start. Those are not polish; a system that guesses confidently and cannot be corrected damages trust in week one.

**Phase 3 — controlled rollout** with quality monitoring in production.

**Phase 4 — expand scope** only once the first slice holds under real traffic.

**Put the uncertainty on the roadmap explicitly.** "Prove policy answers below 2% error" is an honest roadmap item; "AI policy assistant, Q3" hides the fact that the answer might be no.

**Budget for the ongoing work.** Error review, golden-set maintenance, drift watching and model upgrades are recurring, not one-off. A roadmap that allocates no capacity to them is describing a system that will degrade.

title: AI UX
summary: Designing for a system that is usually right, sometimes wrong, and never certain.
what: AI UX is interface design for probabilistic output: setting expectations, showing confidence and provenance, making correction easy, and designing the failure states as carefully as the success state.
why: Conventional UI assumes deterministic behaviour — a button does the same thing every time. When output varies and is sometimes wrong, the interface has to carry information about reliability, and most of the design effort goes into the paths where it did not work.
analogy: A weather forecast. The design communicates uncertainty as a first-class part of the content, not as a disclaimer beneath it.
technical:
The principles that do the work:

**Set expectations before the first interaction.** What it can do, what it cannot, and how sure it is. An unbounded input box implies unbounded capability and guarantees disappointment.

**Show provenance, not confidence scores.** "78% confident" is uninterpretable. A citation the user can open in one click is verifiable, and it converts a trust problem into a checking problem — usually reducing verification from minutes to seconds.

**Design the failure states first.** What happens when it does not know, when retrieval is empty, when the model times out, when the answer is wrong. These paths are a large fraction of real usage and they receive a small fraction of design attention.

**Make correction cheap and make it matter.** One click to flag, visible consequence. A correction mechanism that disappears into a void trains users to stop using it.

**Prefer suggesting to acting** where the cost of error is meaningful. A draft the user edits keeps them in control; an action taken on their behalf transfers the risk to them without their consent.

**Streaming changes perceived performance more than actual latency does.** A first token in 400ms with a 15-second completion feels responsive; five seconds of blank screen with a 6-second completion does not.

**Never present uncertain output with certain-looking formatting.** Fluent, confident prose is the model's default register, and it is the single largest driver of misplaced trust.

title: AI Trust
summary: Trust is earned slowly, lost in two errors, and rebuilt more slowly still.
what: Trust is the user's willingness to rely on the system's output without independently verifying it. It is the variable that determines whether an assistive feature delivers value or merely produces output.
why: A system nobody trusts produces no benefit even when it is correct, because every answer gets checked. Trust is the mechanism by which accuracy becomes value, and it is asymmetric — slow to build, fast to lose.
analogy: A colleague's recommendations. It takes many good calls to be trusted and about two confident wrong ones to be discounted, and after that you are checked forever.
technical:
**The asymmetry is the central fact.** Users tolerate a system that says "I don't know" far better than one that is confidently wrong. An abstention costs a few minutes; a confident error costs the relationship. Our own research figure across support teams is consistent: two confidently wrong answers is the abandonment threshold.

**Calibration matters more than accuracy.** A system that is right 80% of the time and reliably signals which 20% is uncertain is more useful than one right 90% of the time with no signal — because the first can be relied on selectively and the second must be checked entirely.

**Trust is domain-specific and does not transfer.** A user who trusts the summariser does not automatically trust the recommender. Each capability earns it separately.

**Verification cost is the hidden variable.** If checking is cheap, users tolerate more errors, because the error is caught before it costs anything. Reducing verification cost is often more effective than reducing the error rate, and always cheaper.

**Recovery is slower than damage.** After an incident, users check everything for weeks. Rebuilding requires visible change — not "we improved the model" but "here is what went wrong, here is what we changed, here is how you will know".

The practical consequence: **abstention is a trust-building feature, not a limitation.** A system that declines 30% of questions and is right on the rest gets used. One that answers everything at 92% does not.

title: AI Adoption
summary: Getting people to actually use it — which is a different problem from making it work.
what: Adoption is the process by which a working feature becomes part of how people do their jobs. It depends on discoverability, fit with existing workflow, trust, and whether abandoning the old way feels safe.
why: A large share of AI features that meet their quality bar are still not used. Building it correctly and getting it adopted are separate problems, and the second is usually under-resourced because it does not look like product work.
analogy: A new route to work. Genuinely faster, and people keep taking the old one, because the old one is known and the new one has an unquantified risk of being closed.
technical:
The forces, from Jobs To Be Done, apply directly: push, pull, habit and anxiety. **For AI features anxiety is almost always the binding constraint** — capability is obvious and the old way is painful, and people still do not switch because they are not sure they can rely on it.

What actually moves adoption:

**Put it where the work already happens.** A separate tool requires a decision to open it. An affordance inside the existing workflow does not. This single factor dominates most others.

**Make the first experience a success.** Seed it with cases you know it handles. A failure in the first three uses is close to unrecoverable.

**Recruit the sceptics, not the enthusiasts.** Enthusiasts adopt anything and their endorsement persuades nobody. The senior person who was doubtful and then found it useful is the endorsement that moves a team.

**Train on the failure modes, not the features.** Telling people exactly when it will not work makes them trust it more, not less, and it prevents the first surprise from being a betrayal.

**Watch adoption by segment.** Aggregate adoption hides everything. New joiners adopting at 88% and senior staff at 44% is two different products and two different problems.

**Do not mandate.** Enforced usage produces compliance and resentment, and it destroys the signal — you can no longer tell whether the feature is working.

title: AI Metrics
summary: The four layers you have to measure together, because each can be improved by worsening another.
what: AI metrics span four layers: system health, output quality, user behaviour, and business outcome. Each is necessary and none is sufficient, because every one of them can be moved by degrading another.
why: AI features fail in ways conventional monitoring cannot see. Uptime is perfect, error rates are zero, and the product is answering from three-day-old documents. Only a layered metric set catches that.
analogy: A hospital monitoring both the equipment and the patient. Perfectly functioning equipment tells you nothing about whether the patient is recovering.
technical:
**Layer 1 — system.** Availability, p50/p95 latency, error rate, throughput, cost per request. Conventional and necessary.

**Layer 2 — quality.** Groundedness, citation correctness, abstention rate, confidently-wrong rate on sampled production traffic, evaluation scores per release. This is the layer that does not exist unless you build it, and its absence is why AI systems degrade silently.

**Layer 3 — behaviour.** Adoption, queries per user, correction rate, whether users verify elsewhere, whether they retry, whether they abandon mid-task. This is where trust becomes measurable.

**Layer 4 — outcome.** Did the underlying problem shrink? Resolution time, escalations, repeat contacts, the thing the feature was actually for.

**The pairings that matter:** abstention rate against confidently-wrong rate; adoption against correction rate; cost against quality; latency against quality. Every one of these can be improved by worsening its pair, which is why single-metric reporting on AI features is misleading almost by construction.

**Sample production for quality; do not rely on evaluation alone.** Your golden set describes the traffic you anticipated. Production contains the traffic you did not, and the gap widens continuously.

**Track index freshness and corpus version as first-class metrics.** A stale index is the most common silent failure in retrieval systems, and nothing else on any dashboard reveals it.

title: AI Experimentation
summary: Testing changes to a non-deterministic system, where the same input gives different outputs.
what: Experimentation for AI features covers offline evaluation against a fixed set, and online experiments in production — with the complication that the system is stochastic, so identical inputs produce varying outputs.
why: Without a disciplined method, AI iteration becomes prompt-tweaking judged by impression. Teams change something, try three examples, declare improvement, and ship a regression.
analogy: Testing a drug rather than testing a bridge. The bridge either holds or it does not; the drug requires a controlled comparison because the outcome varies between subjects.
technical:
**Offline first.** Every change runs against the golden set before it goes anywhere. It is fast, cheap, reproducible, and it catches most regressions. Fix the seed and temperature where you can, and run multiple samples where you cannot, because a single run of a stochastic system is one draw from a distribution.

**Change one thing.** Prompt, retrieval configuration, model, and chunking all interact. Changing two makes the result uninterpretable, and this is violated constantly because each change individually seems small.

**Report the distribution, not the mean.** A change that raises the average by two points while introducing a new failure mode on edge cases is a regression wearing a promotion's clothes. Look at what got worse, always.

**Then online.** A/B test with real users, on behavioural and outcome metrics — offline quality does not always translate. Guardrail metrics must be included, because a change that improves answer quality and doubles latency can lose overall.

**Ship shadow before you ship live** for anything substantial: run the new configuration alongside the old on real traffic, compare outputs, and expose nobody. It costs inference budget and it is the cheapest way to find out what real traffic does to a change.

**Version everything.** Prompt, model, retrieval config, corpus version. An experiment you cannot reproduce is an anecdote, and the corpus version is the one people forget.

EXPERIMENT = {
    "id": "exp-041",
    "change": "add reranking after retrieval",   # ONE thing
    "baseline": {"prompt": "v7", "model": "sonnet-5",
                 "retrieval": "topk-5", "corpus": "v14"},
    "variant":  {"prompt": "v7", "model": "sonnet-5",
                 "retrieval": "topk-15+rerank-5", "corpus": "v14"},
    "samples_per_case": 3,          # stochastic → repeat
}

def compare(golden, baseline, variant, n=3):
    out = {}
    for name, cfg in (("baseline", baseline), ("variant", variant)):
        per_case = {}
        for case in golden:
            scores = [score(case, run(case, cfg)) for _ in range(n)]
            per_case[case["id"]] = sum(scores) / n
        out[name] = per_case
    return out

# ── THE HEADLINE ───────────────────────────────────────────
# baseline mean 0.784   variant mean 0.806   (+2.2 points)
# → "reranking helps, ship it"

# ── ⚠ THE DISTRIBUTION SAYS OTHERWISE ──────────────────────
improved  = [c for c in GOLDEN if r["variant"][c["id"]] > r["baseline"][c["id"]] + .05]
regressed = [c for c in GOLDEN if r["variant"][c["id"]] < r["baseline"][c["id"]] - .05]

print(len(improved), len(regressed))        # 47 improved, 12 regressed

print(Counter(c["category"] for c in regressed))
# Counter({'not-in-corpus': 11, 'edge': 1})

title: AI Cost
summary: Where the money actually goes, and why the input tokens are usually the bill.
what: AI cost is what it costs to run a feature: model inference, embedding, storage, serving infrastructure, and the human review the system requires to keep working.
why: AI features have a per-request marginal cost that conventional software does not, so unit economics matter from the first user rather than at scale. Teams that estimate on the output size are routinely wrong by an order of magnitude.
analogy: Metered utilities rather than a fixed rent. Every use costs something, so a design decision that adds a little to every request is a permanent tax.
technical:
**Input tokens usually dominate.** A RAG request sends a system prompt, retrieved chunks and conversation history — often several thousand tokens — to produce a two-hundred-token answer. Teams estimate on the answer and are surprised by the bill.

The levers, in rough order of effect:
1. **Send less context.** Retrieve fewer chunks, rerank so fewer are needed, trim history. This is usually the largest and safest saving.
2. **Route by difficulty.** A small model on the easy majority typically cuts blended cost several-fold.
3. **Cache.** Prompt caching for stable prefixes; result caching for repeated questions. In support workloads repeat rates are high.
4. **Cap output.** Set max tokens deliberately rather than by default.
5. **Batch** anything not interactive.

**Count the costs that are not tokens.** Human review of flagged errors, golden-set maintenance and re-embedding after a corpus change are real recurring costs, and they are the ones missing from every early estimate.

**Retries and failures cost full price.** A pipeline that retries twice on 5% of requests costs 10% more than the naive calculation.

**Measure cost per outcome, not per request.** Cost per resolved question is the number that matters. A cheaper model that needs two attempts is not cheaper.

PRICE = {"in": 3.00/1e6, "out": 15.00/1e6}   # per token

def monthly(requests, in_tok, out_tok, *, retry_rate=0.0):
    effective = requests * (1 + retry_rate)
    return round(effective * (in_tok*PRICE["in"] + out_tok*PRICE["out"]))

# ── BASELINE ───────────────────────────────────────────────
print(monthly(240_000, in_tok=5600, out_tok=200, retry_rate=0.05))
# 4,838   (USD/month)
#
# breakdown per request:
#   input   5600 × $3/M  = $0.0168    ← 85% of the cost
#   output   200 × $15/M = $0.0030
#   retries                +5%

# ⚠ THE OUTPUT IS THE EXPENSIVE TOKEN AND THE CHEAP LINE ITEM.
#   Optimising answer length would save ~$150/month.
#   Optimising context would save ~$2,000.

# ── LEVER 1: send less context ─────────────────────────────
# retrieve 15, rerank, send 5 → 4000 chunk tokens becomes 1400
print(monthly(240_000, in_tok=3000, out_tok=200, retry_rate=0.05))
# 2,873   (-41%)
# ⚠ and quality went UP — reranking sends better chunks, not
#   just fewer. This is the rare saving with no trade.

# ── LEVER 2: route by difficulty ───────────────────────────
easy  = monthly(187_000, 3000, 200, retry_rate=0.05) * (0.25/3.00)
hard  = monthly( 53_000, 3000, 200, retry_rate=0.05)
print(round(easy + hard))
# 821    (-83% from baseline)

# ── LEVER 3: prompt caching on the stable prefix ───────────
# system prompt + policy preamble = 1400 tokens, identical
# every request, cached at 10% of the input price
print(round(821 * 0.82))
# 673

# ── ⚠ THE COSTS THAT ARE NOT TOKENS ────────────────────────
NON_TOKEN_MONTHLY = {
    "embedding (corpus updates)":        40,
    "vector storage":                    25,
    "tracing + eval tooling":           180,
    "human error review 3h/wk":         520,   # ← the big one
    "golden-set maintenance 2h/mo":      90,
    "re-embedding on corpus change":    110,   # amortised
}
print(sum(NON_TOKEN_MONTHLY.values()))
# 965   ← MORE than the inference bill after optimisation

# ⚠ THE FEATURE COSTS $673 IN TOKENS AND $965 IN EVERYTHING
#   ELSE. The early estimate counted only the first number,
#   and the human review line is the one that gets cut when
#   budgets tighten — which is the line that keeps it working.

# ── COST PER OUTCOME ───────────────────────────────────────
resolved = 240_000 * 0.71 * 0.83        # answered × accepted
print(round((673 + 965) / resolved, 4))
# 0.0116 per resolved question
# Compare against: 6 minutes of agent time ≈ $0.90
# → ~77x cheaper per resolution. THAT is the business case,
#   and it is a different number from cost per request.

title: AI Latency
summary: Slower than users expect, and the fix is usually perception rather than speed.
what: Latency for AI features is the time from request to useful output. It splits into retrieval, time to first token, generation and post-processing — four components with different causes and different fixes.
why: Generation is inherently slower than a database query, and users compare it to whatever they used before. Latency frequently determines whether a feature is used at all, independently of how good the answers are.
analogy: A conversation versus a lookup. Nobody expects a person to answer instantly and everybody expects a search box to. Which one your interface resembles sets the expectation you will be judged against.
technical:
The components:
- **Retrieval** — tens of milliseconds. Rarely the problem.
- **Time to first token** — prefill, proportional to *input* length. This is what streaming users actually feel.
- **Generation** — proportional to output length, bounded by memory bandwidth.
- **Post-processing** — reranking, validation, safety checks. Additive and easy to overlook.

**Time to first token is the number that matters** for a streaming interface. A 400ms first token with a fifteen-second completion feels responsive; six seconds of blank screen followed by a six-second completion does not. Same total, opposite experience.

The levers: **stream** (the largest perceived improvement available), **shorten the input** (which reduces prefill and cost together — the same lever), **cap output**, **use a smaller model** where quality permits, **parallelise** independent steps, and **cache**.

**Show progress for multi-step work.** An agent making four tool calls over twenty seconds is acceptable when the user can see it working and intolerable behind a spinner.

**Set the expectation with the interface.** A chat interface implies conversational latency; a search box implies instant. Choose the one matching what you can deliver.

**Measure p95, not the mean.** The mean hides the tail, and the tail is what users remember.

def timed_answer(question):
    """One end-to-end number tells you nothing about what to fix."""
    t = {}
    with span("retrieve") as s:
        chunks = retrieve(question, k=15)
    t["retrieve_ms"] = s.ms                        # 42

    with span("rerank") as s:
        chunks = rerank(question, chunks)[:5]
    t["rerank_ms"] = s.ms                          # 180

    stream = generate_stream(question, chunks)
    first = next(stream)
    t["ttft_ms"] = stream.elapsed_ms               # 890
    text = first + "".join(stream)
    t["generation_ms"] = stream.total_ms           # 3100

    t["total_ms"] = sum(t.values())                # 4212

title: AI Risk
summary: What can go wrong, how badly, and which controls actually reduce it.
what: AI risk assessment identifies what can go wrong with a feature, how likely and how severe each failure is, who is harmed, and which controls reduce the risk in practice rather than on paper.
why: AI features fail in ways conventional software does not — fluently, confidently, and without raising an error. That failure mode defeats the usual safeguards, so the risks have to be enumerated deliberately.
analogy: A safety case for a machine. You are not asking whether it works; you are asking what happens on the day it does not, and whether anyone will notice in time.
technical:
The categories:
- **Accuracy risk** — confidently wrong output. The characteristic AI failure.
- **Harm risk** — output that is offensive, discriminatory, defamatory, or dangerous advice.
- **Privacy risk** — data sent where it should not go, or leaked back through output.
- **Security risk** — prompt injection, tool misuse, exfiltration through an agent's capabilities.
- **Compliance risk** — regulated decisions, disclosure obligations, retention.
- **Reputational risk** — a screenshot. Often the binding constraint for consumer products, and frequently the one no framework captures.

**Score severity and detectability, not just likelihood.** A rare, severe, undetectable failure outranks a common, mild, obvious one. Detectability is the axis usually missing, and it is the one AI systems do worst on.

**Controls that actually work** are structural: abstention when unsupported, mandatory citation, human review for consequential actions, capability limits on tools, output filtering, rate limits, and logging sufficient to reconstruct any decision. **Controls that do not work**: disclaimers, "users should verify", and telling the model to be careful in the prompt.

**Consider the agent case separately.** A system that can take actions has a fundamentally larger risk surface than one that only produces text, because a wrong output becomes a wrong action without a human in between.

**Write the kill criteria before launch.** What observation makes you turn this off? Agreeing it in advance is what makes it possible to act during an incident, when nobody wants to be the one who says stop.

questions.q: Why score detectability alongside likelihood and severity?
questions.a: A rare, severe, undetectable failure outranks a common, mild, obvious one. Detectability is the axis usually missing and the one AI systems do worst on, because they fail without raising errors.

questions.q: Why are disclaimers not risk controls?
questions.a: They change nothing about what happens. They transfer blame rather than reduce risk, and a disclaimer on every answer trains people to ignore it.

questions.q: Why write kill criteria before launch?
questions.a: During an incident nobody wants to be the person who says stop. Agreeing the conditions — and who can invoke them without a meeting — in advance is what makes acting possible.

interview.s30: AI risk assessment enumerates what can go wrong, how severe it is, and crucially how detectable it is — because the characteristic AI failure is fluent, confident and silent.
interview.s90: Detectability is the axis I insist on adding, and it reorders the register substantially. On a support assistant, our three highest-scoring risks were all low-detectability: a confidently wrong policy answer, a regional question answered from national policy, and a stale corpus serving withdrawn policy. None of those raises an error, none appears in availability monitoring, and all three would run for days. Meanwhile offensive output — high severity — scored lowest, because it would be visible and reported within minutes. Severity alone would have pointed our effort at the wrong risk entirely. The other thing I do is write kill criteria before launch and name who can invoke them, because a criterion that needs a meeting to trigger will not be triggered — during an incident nobody wants to be the person who says stop.

title: AI Rollout
summary: Releasing gradually, because production contains inputs your evaluation set never had.
what: Rollout is the controlled expansion of an AI feature from a small group to full availability, with quality gates at each stage and a fast route back.
why: Your golden set contains the traffic you anticipated. Production contains the traffic you did not, and the difference is where the failures are. Gradual exposure is how you find that difference cheaply.
analogy: A clinical trial's phases. Not bureaucracy — the recognition that a controlled sample tells you things a laboratory cannot, and that finding them on twenty people is preferable to finding them on twenty thousand.
technical:
The stages, each with an explicit gate:

**Internal** — the team, then adjacent teams. Catches the obvious.
**Shadow** — run on real production traffic, expose nobody, compare outputs against the current behaviour. This is the highest-value stage and the most often skipped, because it produces no visible progress.
**Small cohort** — five to fifteen real users who know they are early, with a direct channel to the team.
**Expanded cohort** — enough for statistical signal on behavioural metrics.
**Full** — with monitoring and kill criteria live.

**Each gate needs numeric criteria agreed in advance**, not a judgement call made under launch pressure.

**A feature flag is not optional.** The ability to turn it off in seconds, per cohort, without a deployment, is what makes gradual rollout safe rather than merely slow.

**Watch the behaviour metrics, not just the quality ones.** The earliest signal of a problem is users starting to verify elsewhere, retry, or abandon — those move before anyone files a complaint.

**Expect the cohort composition to matter.** Early adopters are not representative. A feature that works for the first fifteen enthusiasts can fail at the fiftieth user, who is more sceptical and has different questions.

**Do not expand and change at the same time.** If you widen the cohort and adjust the prompt in the same week, you cannot attribute what happens.

title: The AI PM Decision Checklist
summary: Everything above, in the order you actually need it.
what: A working sequence for taking an AI feature from request to running system, with the question each stage exists to answer and the artefact it produces.
why: The individual practices are each defensible and the order is what makes them work. Most AI feature failures are ordering failures — building before proving feasibility, launching before building evaluation, expanding before the first slice held.
analogy: A pre-flight checklist. Every item is obvious individually, which is exactly why a written sequence exists — the failures come from skipping the obvious under time pressure.
technical:
The sequence, with the question each stage answers:

**1. Is this the right problem?** → a problem statement with a success signal and the cost of a wrong answer.
**2. Is AI the right shape?** → a use-case assessment, or a hybrid reframe.
**3. Can the model actually do it?** → a timeboxed spike with a number and a failure analysis.
**4. What does wrong cost, and how would we know?** → a risk register scored on detectability, and kill criteria.
**5. How will we know if it works?** → a golden set, scoring and a regression harness. Before building the feature.
**6. What is the narrowest useful slice?** → one category, behind a flag, with abstention and error reporting included.
**7. Which model, and what does it cost?** → measured selection by task category; cost per outcome.
**8. How does it fail in front of a user?** → designed failure states, provenance, cheap correction.
**9. Does real traffic look like our evaluation?** → shadow, then cohorts with numeric gates.
**10. Who watches it, forever?** → named owner, weekly review, quality metrics with alerts.

**The two stages that get skipped are 3 and 5**, because neither produces a demo. Skipping stage 3 means building something that cannot work. Skipping stage 5 means never being able to tell whether it does.

**The stage nobody plans for is 10.** An AI feature without a standing owner degrades — the corpus goes stale, errors accumulate unreviewed, and the model stays pinned to whatever launched.

questions.q: Which two stages get skipped, and what does skipping each cost?
questions.a: Feasibility (stage 3) and evaluation infrastructure (stage 5), because neither produces a demo. Skipping the first means building something that cannot work; skipping the second means never knowing whether it does.

questions.q: What is the stage nobody plans for?
questions.a: Standing ownership. Without a named owner running a weekly review, the corpus goes stale, errors accumulate unreviewed, and the model stays pinned to whatever launched.

questions.q: Why is the order the important part?
questions.a: Each practice is individually defensible; most AI feature failures are ordering failures — building before proving feasibility, launching before evaluation exists, expanding before the first slice held.

interview.s30: My sequence for AI features is: right problem, right shape, can the model actually do it, what does wrong cost, how will we know it works — and only then build the narrowest slice. Most failures I have seen are ordering failures rather than execution failures.
interview.s90: The two stages that get skipped are the two that produce no demo: the feasibility spike and the evaluation infrastructure. On the support assistant I worked through, the spike came back at 22.5% confidently wrong, which reads as "not feasible" — but the failure analysis showed six of nine failures were ingestion problems, dropped tables and missing regional documents, not the model. That turned the first two sprints from building the feature into fixing ingestion, and the re-spike came back at 3.1%. Then three weeks of evaluation infrastructure with nothing to show for it, which is the phase that gets cut when a date is under pressure. Fourteen weeks in total, four of them with no visible progress, and those four prevented every failure that would have actually mattered. The stage I now insist on naming explicitly is the last one — who watches this forever — because an AI feature without a standing owner works and then quietly stops.
